author: fester
body: Stage 2. Re-derives the range of every value that enters a bounded slot and requires it to fit the bounds declared there.

author: fester
body: The derivation rules are the ones published in docs/DevelopersGuide.md under Static Bounds Prover, re-implemented here rather than lifted from the compiler's own prover: a second implementation of a published rule is the whole point, and an implementation transcribed from the original inherits the original's misreadings.

author: fester
body: The rechecker does NOT read a node's own type as its derived range. A binary node carries the type of its LEFT OPERAND, so `n * 2` for `n : Integer between 0 and 10` is emitted typed `(int 0 10 ov-error)` while the value's range is 0..20. Trusting node types here would produce a disagreement at almost every arithmetic node and every one of them would be this rechecker's own.

author: fester
body: Products and sums of two full-width bands overflow the arithmetic doing the deriving, which would answer a range narrower than the truth and turn this instrument into a source of false agreement. Anything wider than this guard is answered as unknown instead.

author: fester
body: Containment is the whole judgement of this stage: a value fits a slot when its whole range lies inside the slot's declared band.

author: fester
body: The published table's last row is `let x = v in body` carrying v's range for x in the body. Without it a bounded return written through a let derives from the let name's own type, which for a plain Integer is the full band, and the rechecker reports a disagreement that is entirely its own: `ret-via-let` in codex/test/mod-bound-return did exactly that.

author: fester
body: A binding is pushed only when its range is KNOWN, because an unknown one changes no answer -- the lookup falls back to the name's declared type either way -- and the push is what costs. Lookup runs from the most recent binding backwards so an inner let shadows an outer one of the same name.

author: fester
body: A slot is bounded when its band is narrower than the full width. A plain Integer is a band too, just the widest one, and nothing flows out of it.

author: fester
body: `__narrow` is an explicit runtime-checked assertion, so a value reaching a bounded slot through one is legal whatever its static range: the trap is the contract. It propagates the inner range for anything further up.

author: fester
body: A let-bound range beats the name's declared type; a name the environment does not carry falls back to the type, which is what every name did before the environment existed.

author: fester
body: An application's own type field IS its result type, unlike a binary node's, so a call's range is read from the callee's declared return.

author: fester
body: `int-mod x n` for n > 0 proves [0, n-1] -- the Euclidean remainder, never negative, which is the row `int-rem` does not get. A two-argument builtin arrives curried, so the divisor is the OUTER application's argument and the partially applied inner one is what names the builtin. Its result type on the wire is the builtin's declared plain Integer, so without this rule the value derives to the full band and a provable bounded return is reported as a disagreement.

author: fester
body: A divisor that is not provably positive answers unknown rather than a band that assumes the sign: the published rule is stated for n > 0 and nothing here may widen it.

author: fester
body: Two places a value enters a bounded slot and the wire shows both: an argument arriving at a bounded parameter, and a body arriving at a declared bounded return type.
